subtitle: Practice making advancement paths visible and sharing development opportunities fairly. You will also plan succession on job-related criteria and learn when it is time to bring in HR and labor relations.
audience: For supervisors, managers and HR partners at DHS and DSD who shape assignments, development and succession. Staff interested in their own path will also find it useful.

lessons.title: Making pathways visible
objectives: Explain how job classification specifications and position descriptions shape advancement in Minnesota state service.
Identify at least three ways advancement requirements stay invisible on a team.
Draft a plain-language description of what the next step requires in your unit.
Distinguish what a supervisor can clarify from what only Human Resources can determine.
lessons.teaching:
Knowing your current job does not necessarily explain the requirements of another role. Minnesota state service uses a classification system, so career conversations should connect opportunities with the relevant class specifications and vacancy requirements. Minnesota Management and Budget maintains job classification specifications, organized into career paths and job families, that describe the typical work and qualifications of each class. Each position also has a position description. MMB describes an accurate position description as a Human Resources requirement used primarily for classification and for filling vacancies. In practice, the duties written in a position description, compared against class specifications, are a large part of how a position is classified.

Because the system is technical, requirements for advancement often stay unspoken. Common patterns include: people learn what a promotion requires only by asking someone who already got one; stretch work goes to whoever is closest to the supervisor or whoever asks first; and the difference between being good at your current job and being ready for the next class is never named. These patterns tend to favor people who already have networks, confidence to ask, or time outside work to seek out information. Look for evidence of these patterns in your own unit rather than assuming that they describe every team.

A supervisor can change a lot without touching classification. You can say out loud what advancement in your unit usually requires and write it down. You can walk each person through the class series their position belongs to and point to the public class specifications. Explain relevant experience using current specifications and vacancy requirements, distinguishing required qualifications from useful development. A class series or this application's job-family grouping is not an automatic promotion ladder. You can make sure every person hears this, not only the ones who ask.

Do not promise a reclassification, promotion or pay change before the authorized process is complete. Minnesota Statutes section 43A.07 assigns classification responsibilities to the commissioner; agency HR can identify the applicable delegated authority and review route. Hiring and pay decisions also involve authorized management, rules and agreements. Explain what you can act on and what needs approval, without implying that ordinary supervision transfers entirely to HR.
lessons.keyPoint: Explain current requirements and relevant development opportunities without promising advancement. Use HR to identify the authorized classification process and keep position descriptions accurate.
lessons.example: Practice case: Perpetua has worked as a DSD program consultant for four years and is widely relied on for her knowledge of waiver rules. She asks her supervisor, Leopold, why a colleague hired after her moved into a senior class last year. Leopold realizes he has never explained the class series to anyone on the team. He also suspects Perpetua's current duties may have grown beyond her position description, but he is not sure.
lessons.question: What is the most useful next step for Leopold?
choices: Tell Perpetua he will get her reclassified, since her work clearly deserves it.

Explain the class series and what the senior class typically involves, review her current duties against her position description with her, and bring the question of whether the description needs updating to HR.
Advise Perpetua to apply for outside jobs if she wants advancement, since classification is out of his hands.
feedback: Leopold cannot promise a reclassification. HR can identify the authorized review process; a promise before that process is complete could create misleading expectations.

This is the best response. Leopold closes the information gap, uses what he can influence, which is an accurate position description, and routes the classification question to the people who decide it.
Classification is not his decision, but explaining the pathway and updating the position description are within his role. Sending her away skips steps he can take.
lessons.reflection: When did you first learn what it takes to move up in your current organization? Who told you, and who on your team might not have had that conversation?
lessons.action: Compare your current class specification with a role you want to understand, checking current vacancy requirements where available. Summarize the differences and ask HR about unclear qualifications; a next class is not guaranteed to exist or lead automatically to promotion.

check.question: According to MMB, what is the primary use of a position description?
wrong: Rating employee performance for merit increases.
check.feedback: MMB describes an accurate position description as an HR requirement used primarily for classification and vacancy filling. It can also support performance and training conversations, but its accuracy matters most because it feeds classification decisions.

lessons.title: Fair development: assignments, conversations and sponsorship
objectives: Describe how individual development plans are meant to work under state administrative procedure.
Compare mentoring and sponsorship and when each is useful.
Plan a deliberate rotation of visible assignments on your team.
Identify risks when development tools become hidden records or unpaid labor.
lessons.teaching:
People develop skills through work, so decisions about who receives that work can shape later career options. Who leads the workgroup, who presents to the assistant commissioner, who drafts the legislative report: these assignments build the record that later counts in hiring and promotion decisions. Repeatedly assigning them by habit can limit who has a chance to demonstrate relevant skills.

Minnesota's state administrative procedure on employee learning and development sets an expectation that supervisors and employees jointly discuss, prepare, review and annually update an individual development plan. It describes development as part of performance management and names coaching, mentoring and continuous learning as methods. Used well, an individual development plan is a shared agreement about growth. Discuss development needs openly, including areas for improvement, and give the employee access to the plan through the appropriate process. Agency needs and supervisor approval still apply; a development plan does not guarantee a requested assignment, training or promotion. Follow authorized recordkeeping and access requirements.

Three practices can improve access to development, starting with career conversations for each team member rather than only those who ask. Ask what they want to learn, what kind of work energizes them and what they need to know about the next step. Second, examine access to visible assignments using authorized records. Consider supported opportunities for different staff alongside interest, qualifications, workload, accessibility, continuity and applicable assignment rules; rotation is one possible method, not an entitlement or a substitute for those requirements. Third, understand the difference between mentoring and sponsorship. A mentor gives advice about how rooms work. A sponsor uses their own standing to put someone in those rooms: recommending them for a project, naming their work to leadership or inviting them to a meeting where decisions are made. Both approaches can help, with sponsorship offering a way to expand access to relevant experience. Check whether your recommendations repeatedly draw on the same networks, and use evidence of work rather than familiarity.

Watch for two risks when planning development, starting with reverse mentoring, where a junior staff member teaches a senior leader, can be valuable, but it should not become unpaid equity work expected of staff from underrepresented communities. Do not expect someone to represent a community or disclose personal experiences. Agree on the work, time, workload, support and applicable compensation arrangements; recognize contributions without recording unnecessary identity details. And development plans should not be used as a substitute for classification review when someone is already doing higher-level work.
lessons.keyPoint: Review who receives development opportunities, invite career conversations and provide support. Consider rotation and sponsorship within applicable criteria, workload, access and assignment requirements.
lessons.example: Practice case: Hyacinth supervises nine staff in a DSD provider oversight unit. Reviewing the past year, she sees that the same two analysts presented at every leadership briefing and led both cross-division workgroups. Both are people she worked with before becoming supervisor. A third analyst, Emeka, has quietly written most of the technical content they presented. Hyacinth has an upcoming briefing with the division director. The briefing is an ordinary assignment within Hyacinth's authority, and Emeka can discuss his interest, workload and preparation needs before taking it on.
lessons.question: What should Hyacinth do next?
choices: Ask for volunteers for the briefing at the next staff meeting.
Keep the current presenters, since they have the most experience presenting to leadership.
Talk with Emeka about presenting the briefing, offer preparation support, and start a simple rotation list for visible assignments going forward.
feedback: Asking for volunteers seems open but tends to favor the people already confident with leadership. It does not correct the pattern Hyacinth noticed.
Experience presenting comes from being asked to present. Keeping the same presenters repeats the pattern and keeps Emeka's work invisible.

This is the best response. Hyacinth uses her authority to sponsor Emeka, offers preparation support and creates a way to monitor future access. Neither sponsorship nor a rotation list guarantees success or prevents bias.
lessons.reflection: Who sponsored you, perhaps without calling it that? Whose work on your team is visible to leadership only through someone else's name?
lessons.action: Using authorized records, review access to recent visible assignments. If you supervise, consider an appropriate supported opportunity with someone who has had less access, checking interest, workload and applicable requirements.

check.question: What is the main difference between mentoring and sponsorship?
check.correct: A mentor gives advice and guidance, while a sponsor uses their own standing to create opportunities and advocate for someone.
wrong: Mentoring is formal and paid, while sponsorship is informal and voluntary.
Sponsorship is only for senior leaders, while mentoring is for new employees.
check.feedback: Both can happen at any level and in formal or informal ways. The difference is what the more senior person does: advise, or actively open doors. Both matter, and fair sponsorship reaches beyond the sponsor's own circle.

lessons.title: Succession planning without fit bias
objectives: Explain what succession planning is and why it goes beyond replacing one person.
Identify how judgments of cultural fit can distort talent decisions.
Draft job-related criteria for a critical role before naming possible successors.
Plan a talent pool approach that includes people who want the path, including staff with disabilities.
lessons.teaching:
Succession planning is how an organization prepares for the loss of key people and knowledge. The U.S. Office of Personnel Management describes it as identifying, assessing and developing talent to support continuity, built on workforce analysis, competency modeling and gap analysis. The point is not to crown an heir for each manager. It is to make sure critical knowledge is shared and that several people are developing toward important roles.

Succession planning is also where bias can hide. When leaders are asked who could step into a role, they often name people who remind them of themselves. Sociologist Lauren Rivera studied hiring in elite professional service firms and found that evaluators often weighed cultural similarity, or fit, heavily. They tended to construct merit in their own image, using their own experiences to judge ability, and felt more excitement about candidates who shared their interests. Her study was in a particular private-sector setting, so it does not prove the same thing happens in state government, but the mechanism is familiar. Words like fit, polish, presence and leadership potential can carry a lot of unexamined preference.

One safeguard is to define what the role needs before discussing candidates. Start with the competencies and knowledge the role actually requires, drawn from the position description and the work. Describe each in observable terms: for example, can explain a rule change to county partners in plain language, or has managed a contract through a dispute. Then ask who has shown those things and who could, with development. Build a pool of several people rather than one designated successor. Share the criteria openly so staff know what to build toward.

Include people who have been left out of informal networks. Minnesota Management and Budget guidance on retaining employees with disabilities calls for succession planning that includes a strategy to recruit and retain people with disabilities for the positions and career paths they are interested in. The same logic applies more broadly: ask people what paths they want, instead of assuming. Finally, remember that succession planning is a development tool, not a hiring decision. Formal selection for a vacancy still follows state hiring rules and any labor agreement, and HR is your partner in keeping it fair.
lessons.keyPoint: Define what a role needs in observable terms before naming people, develop a pool rather than an heir, and ask people what paths they want.
lessons.example: Practice case: The DSD leadership team is asked to identify successors for three manager roles expected to open through retirements. In the discussion, one director, Barnaby, says the obvious choice for one role is Declan, who has great presence and fits the team. Another manager, Solveig, notices that no one has described what the role requires, and that two strong analysts who work mostly with Tribal and county partners have not come up at all.
lessons.question: What should Solveig suggest?
choices: That the team first write down the observable competencies each role needs, then consider a pool of candidates against those criteria, including people not yet mentioned.
That Declan be ruled out, since fit-based nominations are biased.
That the team leave succession planning to HR entirely, to avoid bias.
feedback: This is the best response. Setting criteria first makes the discussion about the work, opens the pool and gives Declan and others a fair basis to be considered.
Declan may be well qualified. The problem is the basis for the nomination, not the person. Ruling anyone out is as unfounded as ruling them in.

HR is a key partner, but leaders know the work and are responsible for developing staff. Stepping away does not remove bias. Relevant criteria, consistent evidence and review can reduce the risk, but no single step eliminates bias.
lessons.reflection: When you think of someone as a natural leader, what are you actually noticing? Which of those qualities are required by the work, and which are familiar to you?
lessons.action: Draft four to six observable competencies for a critical role without naming anyone in exercise notes. Use the authorized workforce-planning process for any assessment of identifiable staff, and consider their interests and development needs.

check.question: What did Lauren Rivera's research find about how evaluators judged candidates in elite professional service firms?
check.correct: Evaluators often favored candidates who were culturally similar to themselves and judged merit through their own experiences.
wrong: Evaluators relied almost entirely on structured tests of skills.
Cultural fit had no measurable effect on hiring decisions.
check.feedback: Rivera found that cultural similarity shaped evaluations in those firms. Her study was in a specific setting, so it is a warning about a mechanism, not a measurement of every workplace. Defining job-related criteria first is a practical guard against it.

lessons.title: Acting assignments and knowing when to bring in HR
objectives: Describe what a work out of class assignment is under state administrative procedure.
Explain how acting and interim assignments can open or close advancement opportunities.
Distinguish decisions a supervisor can make from those that need HR, classification or labor relations partners.
Prepare a factual request to HR about an individual advancement concern or a supported pattern, using authorized channels.
lessons.teaching:
Temporary leadership work can build useful skills, but not every acting role is a work out of class assignment. Minnesota Administrative Procedure 17.1 applies when eligible permanent or probationary classified staff perform substantially all duties of a temporarily unoccupied classified position in another class within their agency. This changes the work for a time; it does not appoint the person to the new class. Ask HR which rules apply to the proposed role, including required licenses, posting, pay, time limits and approvals. For probationary staff, agency HR must contact MMB Labor Relations before discussing or offering the assignment. Taking on only some duties may fall outside this procedure, but the work still needs proper authority and review.

Acting roles may provide experience that matters in a later job search, such as leading a team through a difficult change. When those roles repeatedly go to people closest to a departing leader, other staff can miss a chance to learn. Set job-related criteria and use the required process before choosing someone. Consider rotation when the rules and work allow it, rather than treating a turn in the role as something everyone is owed. Explain the process and reasons to the team without sharing private views about other candidates.

A supervisor can discuss career interests, help keep job descriptions accurate and suggest suitable work for staff to learn from. Check the limits of your authority before offering a role, changing pay or making a promise about advancement. HR, labor relations and managers may each have a part in the decision. Their involvement does not remove your duty to explain what you know and follow up on questions.

Bring HR specific concerns as well as wider patterns when they are relevant to the issue. One person's experience may need prompt action even when no pattern has been shown. Share facts through the right channels, keep required records and follow reporting duties. In this learning exercise, leave names and identifying details out of your notes; HR may need those details to handle a real case. Minnesota Statutes section 13.43 distinguishes public personnel data from private data, so a group label does not by itself make information safe to share.
lessons.keyPoint: Use the applicable process for temporary duties and development opportunities. Consult HR about classification, pay and agreement requirements, and raise individual concerns as well as supported patterns.
lessons.example: Practice case: A DSD unit supervisor position will be vacant for several months during a hiring process. The departing supervisor, Wendeline, suggests that her longtime deputy, Ansel, act in the role. The division manager, Priya, knows three other staff have expressed interest in supervision in their career conversations, and one has already led the unit's largest project. Priya wants to fill the gap quickly without repeating an old pattern.
lessons.question: What should Priya do?
choices: Appoint Ansel, since the departing supervisor knows the unit best.

Consult HR about how to structure a work out of class assignment under the relevant labor agreement, define the criteria, and offer the opportunity openly to interested qualified staff, considering rotation if several qualify.
Split the supervisor's duties informally among the three interested staff without any formal assignment.
feedback: Wendeline's view is useful input, but appointing by recommendation alone repeats the pattern of acting roles going to those closest to the departing leader.
This is the best response. Priya uses HR for the parts governed by procedure and contract, sets criteria first and gives interested staff a fair chance at experience that will matter later.
Informal splitting can mean people do higher-level work without recognition, pay rules or clear authority. Substantial higher-level duties raise questions HR should review.
lessons.reflection: Think of acting or interim roles you have seen filled. How was the person chosen, and did others know the opportunity existed?
lessons.action: With your HR partner, find out how work out of class assignments are handled under the labor agreements that cover your team. Write down one practice you will use the next time an interim opportunity arises.

check.question: For ordinary project assignments within established duties and authority, which issue requires a classification review rather than a supervisor deciding alone?
check.correct: Whether a position should be reallocated to a different classification.
wrong: Which team member leads the next visible project.
Holding a career conversation with a staff member.
check.feedback: A classification change needs the authorized review process. An ordinary project assignment or career conversation can be within supervisory authority, but agreement, workload, access or other requirements may still call for consultation.

cards.back: An MMB description of the work associated with a job class. Compare it with current vacancy requirements; application job-family labels do not establish promotion eligibility.
A description of a specific position's duties, used primarily for classification and filling vacancies. Keeping it accurate is a supervisor responsibility.
Using your own standing to create opportunities for someone, such as recommending them for a project or naming their work to leadership.

Under AP 17.1, eligible permanent or probationary classified employees may temporarily perform substantially all duties of an unoccupied classified position in another class within their agency. Check HR requirements before discussion or assignment, especially for probationary employees.
Favoring people who seem culturally similar to decision-makers, often described as fit, polish or presence, rather than using job-related criteria.

aid.heading: What a supervisor can change now
items: Explain current requirements and development options using accurate class and vacancy information; avoid promising advancement.
Hold a career conversation with every person, not only those who ask.
Review access to visible work; consider supported rotation only within assignment rules and operational needs.
Keep position descriptions accurate as duties change.
Recommend supported opportunities using evidence of work, within applicable criteria and authority.

aid.heading: What needs a partner
items: Classification questions and reallocation requests go to HR classification staff.
Pay equity questions go to HR.
Consult labor relations about agreement requirements when needed; keep routine decisions within authorized processes.
Formal selection for a vacancy follows state hiring rules with HR.
Raise individual concerns and supported patterns promptly through authorized channels, sharing necessary facts and protecting personnel data.

aid.heading: Succession planning check
items: Define observable competencies for the role before naming anyone.
Build a pool of several people, not one heir.
Ask people what paths they want instead of assuming.
Include people outside informal networks, including staff with disabilities.
Replace words like fit and presence with the job-related behavior you mean.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — Position Descriptions
sources.note: Supports position descriptions for classification, vacancy filling and everyday supervision; it does not establish that all classification authority rests solely with agency HR.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — Administrative Procedure 17.1, Work Out of Class Assignments (revised 2024)
sources.note: Supports the description of work out of class assignments, pay under labor agreements, time limits and approval rules. Specific terms depend on the applicable agreement, so consult HR.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — Administrative Procedure 21, Employee Learning and Development
sources.note: Supports the expectation that individual development plans are jointly prepared and annually updated as part of performance management.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — Retention (Executive Order 19-15 resources)
sources.note: Supports the recommendation that succession planning include a strategy to recruit and retain people with disabilities for the paths they are interested in. Page contents confirmed by direct retrieval.

sources.title: U.S. Office of Personnel Management — Succession Planning
sources.note: Supports the description of succession planning as identifying, assessing and developing talent for continuity using workforce analysis, competency modeling and gap analysis. Federal guidance, used here for concepts only.

sources.title: Rivera, L. A. — Hiring as Cultural Matching: The Case of Elite Professional Service Firms, American Sociological Review (2012)
sources.note: Supports the finding that evaluators weighed cultural similarity in hiring. The study covered elite private firms and may not generalize to public service; used to illustrate a mechanism.

sources.title: Minnesota Statutes 43A.07 — Classified service
sources.note: Statutory classification authority, review and effects of reclassification; agency HR identifies applicable delegated procedures.

sources.title: Minnesota Statutes 13.43 — Personnel data
sources.note: Distinguishes public and private personnel data. General pattern descriptions do not replace authorized handling of individual concerns.

sources.title: MMB — Job Class Specifications
sources.note: Public class descriptions support comparison of work; learning-platform job families are not a formal promotion ladder.
